clue.text: Selecting a ballad that's cheap

definitions.meaning: read literally, opting for a song: choosing a ballad to perform
the idiom for something sold for very little money

explanation.surface: Someone choosing a ballad that happens to be inexpensive, perhaps sheet music in a sale.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is the phrase taken literally; the second is the idiom for a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: an item sold for a trifling sum is said to change hands for no more than a tune would cost.

clue.text: Say, a cloth picked up in motor home

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the pieces means reading them from the bottom upward

parts.note: EG, short for exempli gratia, means 'say' or 'for example'
a rag is a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: Someone lifting a cloth inside their camper van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' turns EGARAG around. 'motor home' means a home for a motor car, not a camper van.
explanation.definitionFit: A building where a car is kept is jokingly the vehicle's own dwelling.

clue.text: Largely at sea

definitions.meaning: meaning mostly, for the most part
the main is an old word for the open ocean, so this is literally out on the ocean

explanation.surface: Mostly confused and lost, as one might be 'at sea' over something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' looks like 'bewildered' but is meant literally, using the poetic 'main' for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for 'generally' and, literally, describes a ship on the open ocean.

clue.text: Exulted, told age was wrong

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are put wrong, i.e. rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone crowed with triumph after telling another person their age was incorrect.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean took smug, triumphant pleasure in a success.

clue.text: Subeditor here corrected "British Isles"

indicators.note: a subeditor's correction reworks these letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A newspaper subeditor fixing the phrase 'British Isles' in some copy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a plural: these are some of the islands of Britain, not the whole group.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: this Scottish archipelago off the west coast is among the isles belonging to Britain.

clue.text: A Hibernian course

parts.note: the original Scoti were Irish settlers, so a Hibernian (Irishman) can be a Scot; Hibernian is also an Edinburgh football club

explanation.surface: A description of some Irish course, perhaps a racecourse or golf links.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hibernian' looks to mean Irish only; the early Scots came from Ireland. ASCOT is a famous English racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: this Berkshire venue is a racecourse, home of Royal Ascot.

clue.text: First off, burn fuel

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for burn is taken off

parts.note: to boil is to burn, as a fever or rage can boil

explanation.surface: Instructions: first, put out the burner, then deal with the fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First off' looks like 'to begin with' but tells you to remove the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Petroleum is the commonest fuel for engines and heating.

clue.text: Wander about to obtain device

parts.note: to gad about is to wander idly from place to place
to get is to obtain

explanation.surface: Someone roaming around shops in search of a new device.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both mean a small mechanical contrivance or tool.

clue.text: Underground gets new head, consciously old-fashioned

indicators.note: the first letter of the word for underground is replaced with a different one

parts.note: a metro is an underground railway

explanation.surface: A tube line given a new boss, whose style is deliberately dated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets new head' swaps the M of METRO for another letter, R, which the clue leaves unspecified.
explanation.definitionFit: A style deliberately imitating the past is described as harking back, intentionally dated.

clue.text: Amused mark of approval came first

parts.note: a tick is the check mark showing approval
led means was in front, came first

explanation.surface: Someone was pleased to see a tick on their work and to have come top.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: being tickled is being entertained or delighted.

clue.text: Kitchen utensil, I hear, is larger

indicators.note: the speaker hears the word, so its sound gives the letters

parts.note: a grater is a kitchen utensil for shredding cheese

explanation.surface: A boast that some kitchen gadget is the bigger one.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both are comparatives meaning bigger in size.

clue.text: Track down a tiny quantity

definitions.meaning: to find by following clues or a trail

explanation.surface: Someone hunting for a minute amount of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a verb for finding something by following it, and a noun for a minute amount.

clue.text: Very afraid weak crust has collapsed

indicators.note: a collapsed crust has fallen apart, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A baker dreading the moment a fragile pie crust caved in.
explanation.definitionFit: Being overwhelmed with dread or wonder is near-synonymous with being terrified.

clue.text: Intended recipient of notice sees red, being replaced

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a notice

indicators.note: the letters are put back in other places, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: The person a notice was aimed at loses their temper on seeing it put up again.
explanation.definitionFit: The person a letter or message is directed to is its intended recipient.

clue.text: Hair product, counterfeit and low quality, not finished

parts.note: a sham is a fake, a counterfeit

indicators.note: the word lacks its finish, so its last letter goes

parts.note: poor means of low quality

explanation.surface: A complaint about a fake hair product, shoddy and half-made.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a liquid used to wash hair is a common hair product.

clue.text: Tries a drop in house

indicators.note: the pieces sit inside the abbreviation for house

parts.note: to sag is to drop or droop

explanation.surface: Someone attempting a small drink, a drop, at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: making an attempt at something is synonymous with trying it.

clue.text: Area of Somerset no longer low, with river?

parts.note: ex means former, no longer
to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: A query whether some Somerset district has stopped being low-lying, now that a river runs through it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low' looks like an adjective about height but is the cow's call. EXMOOR is a moorland national park in Somerset and Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: this high moorland national park lies largely in Somerset, in south-west England.

clue.text: Relatives found in usual places, commonly

indicators.note: in common, dropped-aitch speech the opening H is not pronounced

parts.note: haunts are the places one usually frequents

explanation.surface: Relatives turning up in the places they usually go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' signals Cockney-style speech, dropping the H of HAUNTS.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: your parents' sisters are among your relatives.

clue.text: Disdain incentive, finally stubborn

parts.note: a spur is an incentive

indicators.note: the final letter of the following word is taken

explanation.surface: An obstinate person who, in the end, scorns any incentive.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms as verbs: both mean reject with contempt.

clue.text: Travelled zigzag courses as told, an imposition on driver

indicators.note: the phrase is told, spoken, so its sound gives the letters

parts.note: rode tacks: a sailor tacks, going in zigzags into the wind

explanation.surface: A motorist weaving about the road, and the charge levied on drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain ROAD TAX is the annual vehicle excise duty paid by car owners.
explanation.definitionFit: A levy charged on owners of cars is a tax imposed on motorists.

clue.text: Unable to sail in a grand circle

parts.note: G is the slang abbreviation for a grand, a thousand
a round is a circle

explanation.surface: A boat stuck in a great circular course, unable to go anywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship stuck on the seabed or shore cannot move under sail.

clue.text: Concerned with following man on the pitch

parts.note: re means about, concerning
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: Someone involved with chasing a footballer on the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: The match official in football is the referee, a figure out on the field of play.

clue.text: Body recently demoted from place ordered out

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names

indicators.note: the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: An official stripped of rank and expelled from their position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered out' reads as 'expelled', but 'ordered' rearranges OUT into UTO.
explanation.definitionFit: This heavenly body was reclassified from planet to dwarf planet in 2006.

clue.text: Mad not to be playing with nursery horse?

definitions.text: not to be playing with nursery horse?
definitions.meaning: a child who has climbed down from a rocking horse is literally no longer on the toy

explanation.surface: Is it crazy to refuse to play with a rocking horse in the nursery?
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the idiom literally: a rocker here is a rocking horse.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for being crazy, taken from someone thrown out of a rocking chair.
